title.en: The Deluge and the Box: Nations Raised from Clay at Tiahuanaco
title.zh: 洪水與箱子:蒂亞瓦納科以泥土造各族

region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤蒂亞瓦納科(今玻利維亞)(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In Molina's fable the deluge drowned all people and things, the water rising above the highest mountains; only a man and a woman in a box survived. When the waters sank the Creator raised each nation from clay at Tiahuanaco, gave it dress, language, song, seeds and food, gave each figure life, and sent the nations underground to emerge from caves, springs, hills and trees.
summary.zh: 莫利納的寓言中,洪水淹沒一切,水高過群山,僅一男一女藏於箱中倖存。水退後,造物主在蒂亞瓦納科以泥土塑造各族,賜予服飾、語言、歌謠、種子與食糧,賦予其生命,再命其入地,分別從洞穴、山泉、丘陵與樹幹中湧出。

sensitivity.note: Quechua creation lore recorded by a Cuzco parish priest c. 1575 from elderly Inca witnesses; a colonial compilation to be read critically. Flood parallels with other traditions are a comparative tagging choice.

passages.text: In the life of Manco Ccapac the painted boards of Poquen Cancha told of the deluge: all people and all created things perished, so that the water rose above all the highest mountains in the world. No living thing survived except a man and a woman who remained in a box, and when the waters subsided the wind carried them to Huanaco, more than seventy leagues from Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: There, in Tiahuanaco, the Creator of all things began to raise up the people and nations of that region, making one of each nation of clay, and painting the dresses that each one was to wear - those who were to wear their hair with hair, and those to be shorn shorn. To each nation he gave the language that was to be spoken, the songs to be sung, and the seeds and food to be sown.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Creator had finished painting and making the nations and figures of clay, he gave life and soul to each one, men and women alike, and ordered that they should pass under the earth. Thence each nation came up in the places to which he had ordered them: some from caves, others from hills, others from fountains, others from the trunks of trees. Because they came forth and multiplied from those places, they made them huacas and places of worship in memory of the origin of their lineages.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Other nations said that in the deluge a few escaped on hills, in caves, or in trees, and that these few began to multiply. In memory of the first of their race who had escaped in such places they made idols of stone, giving to each huaca the name of that first ancestor; and each nation worshipped and offered sacrifices of the things that they used.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, deluge fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Sun Speaks to Manco Capac: The Luminaries Fixed in Heaven
title.zh: 太陽對曼科·卡帕克說話:日月星辰升空

region.en: Island of Titicaca, Lake Titicaca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀湖太陽島(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: It was dark when the Creator, at Tiahuanaco, made the sun, moon and stars and ordered them to the island of Titicaca to rise to heaven. As the sun, in the form of a man, ascended brilliant, it called to Manco Capac: he and his descendants would be lords and subjugate many nations; he was to look on the sun as father. It gave him the suntur-paucar and the champi as arms, and the luminaries took their places in the sky.
summary.zh: 天地尚暗,造物主在蒂亞瓦納科造日月星辰,命其前往的的喀喀島升天。太陽化人形,燦然升空,呼喚曼科·卡帕克:他和子孫將為眾主,征服萬國;當以太陽為父。太陽賜他「孫圖爾-保卡爾」權杖與「昌皮」戰斧等印信武器,日月星辰遂各安其位。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era Quechua fable from Molina's compilation; the solar legitimation of Inca kingship is treated as sacred narrative.

passages.text: They say that it was dark, and that at Tiahuanaco the Creator made the sun, moon, and stars, and that he ordered the sun, moon, and stars to go to the island of Titicaca, which is near at hand, and thence to rise to heaven.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, solar fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: They also declare that when the sun, in the form of a man, was ascending into heaven, very brilliant, it called to the Yncas and to Manco Ccapac as their chief, and said: 'Thou and thy descendants are to be Lords, and are to subjugate many nations. Look upon me as thy father, and thou shalt be my children, and thou shalt worship me as thy father.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, solar fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: With these words the sun gave to Manco Ccapac, for his insignia and arms, the suntur-paucar and the champi, and the other ensigns used by the Yncas like sceptres. At that point the sun, moon, and stars were commanded to ascend to heaven and fix themselves in their places, and they did so. At the same instant Manco Ccapac and his brothers and sisters, by command of the Creator, descended under the earth and came out again in the cave of Paccari-tambo, at the point where the sun rose on the first day after the Creator had divided night from day. Thus they were called children of the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, solar fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Disobedient Turned to Stone: Fire from Heaven at Pucara
title.zh: 不從者化石:普卡拉的天火

region.en: Pucara on the Collao road, Collasuyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科利亞道上的普卡拉(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: After peopling the nations the Creator walked the mountain road reviewing his work. Finding nations that had rebelled against his commands, he turned many of them into stones in the shape of men and women wearing their own dress - at Tiahuanaco, Pucara, Xauxa, Pachacamac and Cajamarca, where the huaca Huarivilca too was petrified. At Pucara fire came down from heaven and destroyed part of the people, and the fleeing were turned to stone.
summary.zh: 造物主造畫各族後,沿山路巡視所造之民。發現有族不服其命,便將許多石化為人形石塊,仍著其衣——蒂亞瓦納科、普卡拉、豪哈、帕查卡馬克、卡哈馬卡等處皆然,連瓦里維爾卡瓦卡也被石化。在普卡拉,天火降下,毀去部分人民,奔逃者亦化為石。

sensitivity.note: Colonial-era fable explaining the standing monoliths of the Collao road; Molina rationalizes them as Roman work while preserving the native tale.

passages.text: The Creator, called Pachayachachi and Tecsiviracocha, the incomprehensible God, went by the road of the mountains from Tiahuanaco, visiting and beholding all the nations, and examining how they had begun to multiply and to comply with his commands. He found that some nations had rebelled and had not obeyed his commands, so he turned a large number of them into stones in the shape of men and women, with the same dress that they had worn. These conversions into stone were made at Tiahuanaco, at Pucara, at Xauxa - where they say he turned the huaca called Huarivilca into stone - and at Pachacamac and Cajamarca, and in other parts.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, stone fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: In truth there are great blocks of stone in those places, some nearly the size of giants, made by human hands in very ancient times; and by reason of the loss of memory and the absence of writing the people invented this fable, saying that people had been turned into stones for their disobedience by command of the Creator. They also relate that in Pucara, forty leagues from Cuzco on the Collao road, fire came down from heaven and destroyed a great part of the people, while those taking to flight were turned into stones.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, stone fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Ymaymana and Tocapo: The Two Sons Name the World
title.zh: 伊馬伊馬納與托卡波:二子命名世界

region.en: Highland and lowland roads from Tiahuanaco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自蒂亞瓦納科出的山路與平地之路(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Creator had two sons, Ymaymana Viracocha, in whose power all things were placed, and Tocapo Viracocha, 'the maker'. The elder was sent by the mountain and forest roads to name every tree, flower and fruit, teaching which were food or medicine and which poison; the younger went by the plains, naming rivers and trees and teaching their fruits. Thus they went until they reached the sea, whence they ascended to heaven.
summary.zh: 造物主有二子:長子伊馬伊馬納·維拉科查,萬物皆在其掌中;次子托卡波·維拉科查,意為「造者」。長子奉命循山路林道而行,為大小樹木、花卉果實命名,教人何者可食可藥、何者有毒;次子循平地而行,為江河樹木命名,教導花果之性。二人行至海濱,遂自海中升天。

sensitivity.note: Naming-journey fable recorded by Molina; tagged as a culture-hero and sibling pair against the comparative clusters.

passages.text: They also have another fable, in which they say that the Creator had two sons, the one called Ymaymana Viracocha, and the other Tocapo Viracocha. Having completed the tribes and nations, and assigned dresses and languages to them, the Creator sent the sun up to heaven with the moon and stars, each one in its place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, two-sons fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Creator commanded that the elder, named Ymaymana Viracocha, in whose power all things were placed, should set out and go by the way of the mountains and forests through all the land, giving names to the large and small trees, and to the flowers and fruits that they bear, and teaching the people which were good for food or for medicine, and which should be avoided. He also gave names to all the herbs, and explained which had healing virtues and which were poisonous.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, two-sons fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The other son, named Tocapo Viracocha, which means 'the maker', was ordered to go by the way of the plains, visiting the people, and giving names to the rivers and trees, and instruction respecting the fruits and flowers. Thus they went until they reached the sea, whence they ascended to heaven, after having accomplished all they had to do in this world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, two-sons fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Birds Given Their Songs: Beasts and Reptiles Made at Tiahuanaco
title.zh: 賦鳥以歌:蒂亞瓦納科造鳥獸蟲蛇

region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤蒂亞瓦納科(今玻利維亞)(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At Tiahuanaco, where all mankind was created, all the different kinds of birds were made, male and female, and each was given the songs it was to sing; those that were to live in the forest were sent there, and each kind to its place. In like manner all beasts, serpents and lizards were created, and the people were taught the names and qualities of every one.
summary.zh: 在造出全人類的蒂亞瓦納科,各類鳥也被造出,雌雄皆有,並各賜其當唱之歌;將棲於林中的被送往林間,各歸其所。野獸、蛇、蜥蜴亦如是造成,並教人民認識每一種的名字與習性。

sensitivity.note: Fragment of the Tiahuanaco creation cycle in Molina's compilation.

passages.text: They also relate, in this same fable, that at Tiahuanaco, where all mankind was created, all the different kinds of birds were made, male and female, and that each was given the songs they were to sing; those that were to live in the forest being sent there, and each kind to its respective place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: In like manner all the different beasts were created, male and female, and all the serpents and lizards that are met with in the land; and the people were taught the names and qualities of each of these birds, beasts, and reptiles. These Indians believed for a certainty that neither the Creator nor his sons were born of woman, that they were unchangeable and eternal.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Cañari Brothers and the Macaw Wives
title.zh: 卡尼亞里兄弟與金剛鸚鵡之妻

region.en: Cañaribamba (Cañar), province of Quito, Ecuador (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 基多省卡尼亞里班巴(今厄瓜多卡尼亞爾)(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In the flood the Cañari brothers escaped to the mountain Huaca-yñan, which grew with the waters. Starving after the flood, they found their hut daily stocked with food and chicha they had not prepared. Watching from hiding, they saw two macaws come dressed as Cañari women, hair bound in front, and cook for them; seized in the hut, the smaller macaw became their wife and bore six sons and daughters, from whom all the Cañaris descend. They hold the hill Huaca-yñan as a huaca and revere macaws, valuing their feathers for festivals.
summary.zh: 洪水時,卡尼亞里二兄弟逃上山瓦卡伊尼亞,山隨水而高,洪水不至。水退後二人飢寒交迫,卻見屋中每日備有食物與奇恰酒。二人先後藏匿窺看,見兩隻金剛鸚鵡化作卡尼亞里女子,前束髮髻,為其炊食。二人閉門捕捉,小鸚鵡被擒,遂為其妻,生六子女——卡尼亞里人皆其後裔。故奉瓦卡伊尼亞山為瓦卡,尊崇金剛鸚鵡,節慶時珍用其羽。

sensitivity.note: Etiological ancestor tale of the Cañari nation; recorded within Molina's compilation.

passages.text: The Cañaris say that at the time of the deluge two brothers escaped to a very high mountain called Huaca-yñan. As the waters rose the hill also increased in height, so that the waters never reached them. After the flood had subsided their store of provisions being ended, they came forth and sought food in the hills and valleys. They built a very small house in which they dwelt, living on herbs and roots, and suffering much from hunger and fatigue.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, after going out in search of food, they returned and found food to eat and chicha to drink, without knowing who could have prepared it. This happened for ten days. They consulted how they should see the being who did them so much good, and the elder brother agreed to remain concealed. Presently he saw two birds of the kind called guacamayos, dressed as Cañaris, with their hair fastened in front as they now wear it. They began to prepare the food they had brought, the larger one taking off the lliclla or mantle worn by the Indians.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the concealed man saw that they were beautiful, and had the faces of women, he came forth; but as soon as they saw him they were enraged and flew away without leaving anything to eat that day. On the next day the younger brother resolved to watch. At the end of three days the two guacamayos came back and began to prepare the food; the men watched for an opportune time, and, shutting the door, enclosed them inside. The birds showed great anger; but while they held the smaller one the larger went away.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they had carnal knowledge of the smaller one, and had by it six sons and daughters. It lived with them for a long time on that hill, and they subsisted on the seeds they sowed, which were brought by the guacamayo. From these brothers and sisters, children of the guacamayo, all the Cañaris proceed. Hence they look upon the hill Huaca-yñan as a huaca, and hold the guacamayos in great veneration, valuing their feathers for use at their festivals.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Cañari fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Sheep that Watched the Stars: Ancasmarca and the Flood
title.zh: 凝望星辰的羊群:安卡斯馬爾卡與洪水

region.zh: 庫斯科附近安蒂蘇尤安卡斯馬爾卡(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: A month before the flood the sheep of Ancasmarca grew sad, eating nothing by day and watching the stars by night. Asked what ailed them, they said the conjunction of stars showed the world would be destroyed by water. The shepherd consulted his six children, they gathered all the food and sheep they could, and climbed the very high mountain called Ancasmarca; the hill rose with the waters so the flood never covered them, and sank again when the waters sank. The six children returned and repeopled the province.
summary.zh: 洪水來前一個月,安卡斯馬爾卡的羊群終日不吃,夜夜望星。牧人問其故,羊答:星辰會合之象顯示世界將毀於水。牧人與六子商議,收集所有食物羊隻,登上一座極高的名為安卡斯馬爾卡之山。水漲山亦漲,洪水不得掩之;水退山亦減。六子下山,重造此省之民。

sensitivity.note: Animal-omen flood tale from Molina's compilation; the speaking sheep motif is compared across traditions.

passages.text: In the province of Ancasmarca, five leagues from Cuzco in the Anti-suyu division, they say that a month before the flood came their sheep displayed much sadness, eating no food in the day-time, and watching the stars at night. At last the shepherd who had charge of them asked what ailed them, and they said that the conjunction of stars showed that the world would be destroyed by water. When he heard this, the shepherd consulted with his six children, and they agreed to collect all the food and sheep they could, and to go to the top of a very high mountain called Ancasmarca. As the waters rose, the hill grew higher, so that it was never covered by the flood; and when the waters subsided, the hill also grew smaller. Thus the six children of that shepherd returned to people the province.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Ancasmarca fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Sun Cannot Be God: Inca Yupanqui Builds a Temple to the Creator
title.zh: 太陽不會是神:印加·尤潘琪建造物主神廟

region.zh: 庫斯科基蘇瓦爾坎恰(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Yupanqui, who first regulated the twelve months and their ceremonies, reasoned with his council that the Sun could not be the God who created all things: the sun never rests and journeys round the earth daily, and permits a small cloud to obscure his splendour. There must be someone who directs him - the Pachayachachi, the Creator. He therefore raised at Quisuar-cancha a golden statue of the Creator, a boy of ten years with right arm raised as if giving orders, ordered temples, flocks and estates throughout the empire, and sumptuously rebuilt the house of the Sun.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪首定十二月之歲與其祭儀。他與眾臣論道:太陽不得為造萬物之神——太陽無一刻休息,日日繞地而行,還容許一小片雲遮其光輝。若太陽真是造物主,必當安坐一處,光照世界。故必有指揮太陽者,即造物主帕查亞查奇。他在基蘇瓦爾坎恰立一尊十歲孩童大小的造物主金像,右手高舉如發號施令;又令各行省建廟、置畜群莊園以供祭祀,並華美重建太陽神廟。

sensitivity.note: Theological-reflection fable attached to Inca Yupanqui (Pachacuti); a colonial-era compilation to be read critically.

passages.text: It was this Ynca who first began to conquer this land... He appears to have been the first to order and settle ceremonies and religions. He established the twelve months of the year, giving a name to each and ordaining the ceremonies to be observed in each; although his ancestors used months and years counted by the quipus, they were never before regulated in such order.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was of such clear understanding that he reflected upon the reverence shown by his ancestors to the Sun, whom they worshipped as God. He observed that the Sun never had any rest, and daily journeyed round the earth; and he said to his council that it was not possible that the Sun could be the God who created all things, for if he were, he would not permit a small cloud to obscure his splendour; and if he were creator of all things he would sometimes rest, and light up the whole world from one spot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thus, it cannot be otherwise but that there is someone who directs him, and this is the Pacha-Yachachi or Creator. Influenced by this reasoning, he ordered the houses and temple of Quisuar-cancha to be made, where he raised a statue of gold to the Creator of the size of a boy of ten years - a man standing up, the right arm raised, the hand almost closed, the fingers and thumb raised as one who was giving an order. He gave orders to the heads of provinces that temples should be erected to him, with flocks, servants, farms and estates for sacrifices; and he sumptuously erected the house of the Sun at Cuzco, which before his time had been very small and poor.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Crystal in the Fountain: The Apparition at Susur-puquio
title.zh: 泉中水晶:蘇蘇爾普基奧的顯靈

region.zh: 夏基夏瓜納附近蘇蘇爾普基奧泉(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Before his succession Inca Yupanqui, going to visit his father Viracocha Inca at Sacsahuana, saw a piece of crystal fall into the fountain of Susur-puquio, within which he beheld a figure: three brilliant sun-like rays from the back of the head, serpents twined round the arms, a llautu like an Inca's, ear-pieces, a lion's head between the legs and lions over the shoulders. He fled, but the apparition called him by name: 'Come hither, my son, and fear not, for I am the Sun thy father. Thou shalt conquer many nations.' It vanished, leaving the crystal, in which he afterwards saw everything he wanted; he then had a statue of the Sun made resembling the figure.
summary.zh: 印加·尤潘琪繼位前,赴薩克薩瓦納看望父親維拉科查·印加,途經蘇蘇爾普基奧泉,見一水晶落入泉中,內現神人:腦後射出三道如日光芒,雙臂纏蛇,額繫印加之「勞圖」,耳垂穿孔佩耳飾,裝束一如印加;兩腿間現獅首,肩上伏獅,肩後又有蛇纏。尤潘琪驚逃,神影自泉中喚其名:「來吧,吾子,勿懼——我是太陽,你的父親。你將征服許多國度;務必崇敬我,祭祀勿忘。」神影隨即消失,水晶留存。尤潘琪藏之,日後凡有所求,皆於水晶中得見。繼位後,他命工匠依泉中所見造太陽金像,並命各行省為太陽建廟,令民眾尊崇新神。

sensitivity.note: Vision fable attached to Inca Yupanqui; the crystal motif parallels scrying traditions elsewhere.

passages.text: They say that, before he succeeded, he went one day to visit his father Viracocha Ynca, who was in Sacsahuana, five leagues from Cuzco. As he came up to a fountain called Susur-puquio, he saw a piece of crystal fall into it, within which he beheld the figure of an Indian in the following shape: out of the back of his head there issued three very brilliant rays like those of the Sun; serpents were twined round his arms, and on his head there was a llautu like that of the Ynca. His ears were bored, and ear-pieces like those used by the Yncas were inserted; he was also dressed like the Ynca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Susur-puquio fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The head of a lion came out from between his legs, and on his shoulders there was another lion whose legs appeared to join over the shoulders of the man, while a sort of serpent also twined over the shoulders. On seeing this figure the Ynca Yupanqui fled, but the figure called him by his name from within the fountain, saying: 'Come hither, my son, and fear not, for I am the Sun thy father. Thou shalt conquer many nations: therefore be careful to pay great reverence to me, and remember me in thy sacrifices.' The apparition then vanished, while the piece of crystal remained.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Susur-puquio fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Ynca took care of it, and they say that he afterwards saw everything he wanted in it. As soon as he was Lord, he ordered a statue of the Sun to be made as nearly as possible resembling the figure he had seen in the crystal, gave orders to the heads of the provinces in all the lands he had conquered that they should make grand temples richly endowed, and commanded all his subjects to adore and reverence the new Deity as they had heretofore worshipped the Creator. He also caused worship to be offered to the thunder, and had a statue of a man erected in gold in a temple in the city of Cuzco.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, Susur-puquio fable (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Five Orders of Diviners: Tubes, Flames, Maize and Thunder
title.zh: 五等占卜師:銅管、火焰、玉米與雷

region.zh: 庫斯科及各行省(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Molina lists the classes of wizards: Calparicu, who blew up the lungs of sacrificed birds and lambs to read signs of what was to come; Virapiricuc, who burned sheep's breasts and coca and divined from the burning - though those who consulted them said they always lied; Achicoc, who told fortunes by maize and sheep's dung, odd or even; Camascas, whose grace came from the thunder that struck them and revealed herb-curing; and Yacarcaes of Huaro, who blew charcoal fires through copper tubes until the devils delivered replies in the flames - asking whether a man was against the Sun his father, a thief, murderer or adulterer. By this invocation the Inca knew all that passed in his dominions.
summary.zh: 莫利納記各類巫師:一、卡爾帕里庫,剖祭鳥祭羊之肺吹脹視其徵兆;二、維拉皮里庫庫,焚羊乳與古柯,觀火焰占卜——求問者稱其「常常說謊」;三、阿奇科克,以玉米粒與羊糞占吉凶,視奇偶而定;四、卡馬斯卡,稱其法力得自雷霆——遭雷擊而復甦者,自言雷神授其草藥醫術;五、瓦羅地方的亞卡爾卡埃斯,以銅管吹旺炭火,魔鬼便在火中作答——所問者,某人是否違逆太陽之父、是否盜賊、兇手、姦夫。印加王借此召問,盡知帝國內所發生之事,故常攜其同行。

sensitivity.note: Ethnographic taxonomy of Quechua diviners; 'devil' is the missionary translation of native huaca-speaking.

passages.text: There were many kinds of wizards in the provinces, with names and attributes differing one from the other. Calparicu means those who bring luck and success, who were expected to obtain the things that were desired; they killed birds, lambs, and sheep, and, inflating the lungs through a certain vein, discerned signs of what was about to happen. Others, called Virapiricuc, burnt the breasts of sheep and coca in the fire and foretold from signs at the burning - though those who consulted them said they were the least to be relied on, because they always lied.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, wizards section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Others were called Achicoc, sorcerers that told fortunes by maize and the dung of sheep, giving replies according as the things came out in odd or even numbers. Others were called Camascas, who declared their grace and virtue came from the thunder: when a thunderbolt fell and one of them was struck with terror, after he came to himself he proclaimed how the thunder had revealed to him the art of curing by herbs and how to give replies to those who consulted them; hence many Indians are great herbalists.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, wizards section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Others were called Yacarcaes, natives of Huaro, who had mighty pacts with the devil. They took tubes of copper mixed with silver, about the length of an arquebus, and brass vessels in which they lighted charcoal fires, which they blew and made to blaze up by means of the tubes. In these fires the devils delivered their replies, and the sorcerers said they were inquiring concerning the soul of such a man or woman, who might be in Quito or in any other part of the empire. The principal questions were whether such an one was against the Sun his father, or whether such others were thieves, murderers, or adulterers. By this invocation the Ynca knew all that passed in his dominions, and took the Yacarcaes with him wherever he went.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, wizards section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Confession to the Keepers of the Huacas

region.zh: 瓦羅與庫斯科(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Recorded by Cristóbal de Molina at Cuzco, c. 1575; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Molina of Cuzco, 'An Account of the Fables and Rites of the Yncas', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: All the people of the land confessed to the sorcerers who had charge of the huacas, and these confessions were made publicly; the priests tested them by signs and, with the aid of the speaking huaca, discovered who had confessed falsely and punished them severely. Grave crimes were confessed in secret. The Incas and people of Cuzco confessed in secret to the sorcerers of Huaro, accusing themselves of failing to reverence the sun, moon and huacas, of not celebrating the Raymi feasts with all their heart, of seducing a virgin not given by the Inca, of theft, murder, and of murmuring against the Inca or the Sun.
summary.zh: 全境人民皆向掌管瓦卡的祭司懺悔,懺悔公開舉行;祭司以徵兆驗其真偽,藉瓦卡之言查出謊供者,嚴加懲處。重罪者則私下密供。印加王室與庫斯科人皆向瓦羅祭司密懺,自陳不敬日月瓦卡、未全心慶祝雷米祭、姦污非印加所賜之處女、盜竊、殺人,以及對印加王或太陽之怨言。

sensitivity.note: Description of Andean confession practice from a priest-observer; his moral framing ('fornication against the law of the Ynca') is quoted critically.

passages.text: All the people of the land confessed to the sorcerers who had charge of the huacas, and these confessions were made publicly. In order to test the truth of the confessions, the sorcerers tried them by consulting signs, and in this way they discovered who had confessed falsely, and upon these they inflicted severe punishments. Those who had grave crimes to confess, which merited death, confessed them in secret to the sorcerer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, confession section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Yncas and the people of Cuzco always made their confessions in secret, generally to the Indian sorcerers of Huaro. In their confessions they accused themselves of not having reverenced the sun, the moon, and the huacas; of not having celebrated the feasts of the Raymis with all their hearts; of having committed fornication against the law of the Ynca not to touch a strange woman or seduce a virgin unless given by the Ynca - and not because fornication was a sin, for they did not understand this. They also accused themselves of any murder or theft, and of murmurs, especially if against the Ynca or against the Sun.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Molina, Fables and Rites, confession section (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)
